title: The American Station of the Notated Body — San Francisco to Monterey
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: La Débutante — The Actress Is Made (1857–1876)

stops.name: San Francisco — the birth on the far shore
stops.campa: On 7 March 1857, in the young gold-rush city on the Pacific rim, Geneviève Stebbins is born to the lawyer James Cole Stebbins, of upstate New York, and his wife Henrietta. The child comes into the world at the continent's farthest western edge, a whole nation away from the stages that will make her. Before she is two her mother fails and dies; the girl is given over to the care of her aunt Louisa. From the first she loves to dance and to perform — the body, not the book, is her native tongue.
suggested_refs: Portrait of Genevieve Stebbins (New York School of Expression prospectus)

stops.name: New York — Union Square Theatre, the leading juvenile
stops.campa: Grown, she crosses the continent to New York to study for the stage. Under a leading actress of Albert Marshman Palmer's company at the Union Square Theatre she serves a winter's apprenticeship, then makes her debut as the leading juvenile in Rose Michel. She is engaged afterward under Dion Boucicault and plays in Our Boys at Daly's. The gaslit theatres of Union Square are her first temple; the mechanics of feeling shown outward through the body are the mystery she is being trained to serve.
suggested_refs: Union Square Theatre playbill, Rose Michel

segments.name: La Transmission Delsartienne — The System Received Through Mackaye (1876–1880)

stops.name: New York — Steele Mackaye lays the system upon her
stops.campa: At Daly's she meets Steele Mackaye, the one American who sat at the feet of François Delsarte in Paris and carried the master's laws of expression home across the ocean. Mackaye persuades her to leave the stage and give herself wholly to the science of gesture. For two years she studies under his hand the Delsarte System — the trinity of life, mind and soul written in the body; the nine laws of gesture; the decomposing exercises that free each part of the frame in turn. The living link is forged: Delsarte's laws pass, through Mackaye's hands, into hers.
stops.quote: When before the public in the pulpit, on the platform, or the stage, forget all rules, or rather make no effort to recall them. Your motto there should be heart-work, not head-work.
stops.quote_source: Genevieve Stebbins, Delsarte System of Expression (1885)
suggested_refs: Delsarte System of Expression (1885), title page

stops.name: Boston — the School of Oratory, Mackaye's representative
stops.campa: For six months of her novitiate she goes to Boston as Mackaye's representative at the Boston University School of Oratory, giving the Delsarte system to pupils and teachers in exchange for lessons in elocution from Professor Richard McCurdy. She is given full charge of the Delsarte program. Here the transmission turns outward for the first time: she is no longer only a vessel of the system but its teacher, and the classes multiply — the Ethical Society, the Kindergarten Society, the musical clubs all send their bodies to be reformed by the laws of expression.
suggested_refs: Boston University School of Oratory records

stops.name: Boston — Mary S. Thompson, the fourteen-year partner
stops.campa: At the School of Oratory in 1878 she is admitted to a vocal-training course taught by Mary S. Thompson, and finds in her the collaborator of the next fourteen years. Voice and gesture join hands. The two women will carry the Delsarte matinee up and down the eastern seaboard together, Thompson's science of the breathing voice braided into Stebbins's science of the moving body. The partnership that will build the New York School of Expression is founded here, in a Boston classroom.

segments.name: Le Voyage à la Source — Paris and the Return to the Stage (1879–1882)

stops.name: New York — Madison Square Theatre, the return as leading lady
stops.campa: In May 1879, her two years of Delsarte study finished, she re-enters the stage as leading lady of the Madison Square Theatre. The training has changed her: she moves now by a science, every attitude answering to a law. The following year she accepts an engagement for Shakespearean roles. But the stage no longer holds her whole ambition; the system she has received has opened a hunger to go back to its wellspring, to the country of Delsarte himself, and drink at the source.

stops.name: Paris — study with Regnier at the Théâtre-Français
stops.campa: In 1881 she crosses to Paris, to the source. There she studies under François-Joseph Regnier, sociétaire of the Comédie-Française and President of the Conservatoire — the great school of the classic French stage where Delsarte himself once taught and rebelled. In the Théâtre-Français she takes the discipline of the tradition into her own body, back at the fountainhead of the laws Mackaye had carried west. The pilgrimage to the master's country completes what the transmission began: she has now touched the living root of the art.

stops.name: New York — the return, and the turn to teaching
stops.campa: In 1882 she returns to the United States, reads in public and takes theatrical engagements, but the current of her life is turning. The stage was the school; teaching is to be the temple. She becomes a special instructor in twenty-one New York schools, carrying the reformed body into the education of the young. The actress is becoming the founder of a system — no longer content to embody the laws of expression, she will now codify them, name a new gymnastics, and give it to a generation of women.
suggested_refs: New York public schools, physical culture, 1880s

segments.name: Le Livre et la Gymnastique — The Manuals and the New System (1885–1892)

stops.name: New York — the Delsarte System of Expression is published
stops.campa: In 1885 she brings forth her first book, the Delsarte System of Expression. Its opening word — 'This is an age of formulations' — announces her mission: to fix in print the laws that Delsarte left scattered and unwritten, that Mackaye taught by voice alone. The book's success decides her whole future. She will be a lecturer and a teacher; the system will be canon. From this text the American Delsarte movement takes its scripture, and the reformed body its first American gospel.
stops.quote: This is an age of formulations.
stops.quote_source: Genevieve Stebbins, Delsarte System of Expression (1885)

stops.name: New York — the solo dances, the Goddess Isis rises
stops.campa: In 1887, her decade of acting behind her, she begins to perform solo dances — dramatic movement and expressive gesture made to portray the very idols of antiquity. She dances the Goddess Isis. Draped in the flowing chiton, she rises out of stillness into a slow rhythmic unfolding of every part of the body, the statue coming to life. This is the birth of what the age will call her 'statue-posing' and her 'artistic attitudes': the Greek and Egyptian forms made to breathe. The living tableau is born.
suggested_refs: Genevieve Stebbins in chiton, statue-posing photographs

stops.name: New York — Madison Square Theatre, the first Delsarte Matinee
stops.campa: In February 1888 Stebbins and Mary Thompson present their first Delsarte Matinee at the Madison Square Theatre. Before the fashionable audiences of Gilded-Age New York the statue-poses flow gracefully onward from the simple to the complex, commencing with a single attitude and continuing with a slow rhythmic motion of every portion of the body. The pantomimes illustrate a poem, a story, a myth. The lecture-demonstration is invented as a form: the body shown as an instrument of expression, its laws made visible to the paying public.
suggested_refs: Delsarte Matinee playbill, Madison Square Theatre, 1888

stops.name: New York — Society Gymnastics and Voice-Culture
stops.campa: In 1888 appears her second book, Society Gymnastics and Voice-Culture, Adapted from the Delsarte System — the drawing-room made a gymnasium. Here she carries the reform of the body to the parlors of society women, teaching poise, breath and grace as culture. The physical-culture woman is being invented, and Stebbins is her maker: the pupil-list will come to hold Mrs. Pierpont Morgan and Mrs. John D. Rockefeller. The reformed body becomes a mark of refinement, and the Delsarte drill enters the American home.

stops.name: Harvard — the Summer School, the Swedish gymnastics gathered in
stops.campa: She makes trips abroad to perfect her system and studies at home with Dr. George H. Taylor the Swedish Ling medical and pedagogical gymnastics. In the summer of 1892 she attends the Harvard Summer School for Swedish educational gymnastics and aesthetic dance. Into the Delsarte laws of expression she now weaves the Ling drills of the Swedish reformers, the German physical culture, and the yogic breath she has met — the harmonic gymnastics is being compounded out of many traditions into a single new thing, hers alone.
suggested_refs: Harvard Summer School of Physical Education
Dr. George H. Taylor, Swedish Movement Cure

stops.name: New York — Dynamic Breathing and Harmonic Gymnastics
stops.campa: In 1892 she publishes the keystone work — Dynamic Breathing and Harmonic Gymnastics: A Complete System of Psychical, Aesthetic and Physical Culture. Here the breath is set as the ground of all movement: the dynamic breath is the current out of which gesture rises, the psychical made physical. To it she appends her nine-point credo, the distillation of decades. This is the invention proper — Harmonic Gymnastics, the Delsarte laws married to breath and to the aesthetic drill. The current is loosed that will run into the whole of modern dance.

segments.name: L'École et les Attitudes Grecques — The School and the Greater Eleusinia (1892–1907)

stops.name: New York — Madison Square Theatre, the Dance of Day
stops.campa: At a Delsarte matinee at the Madison Square Theatre, given for the National Christian League for the benefit of social purity, Stebbins performs The Dance of Day — classical poses fused with rhythmic motion to evoke the turning of the natural cycle. In the audience sits a young woman named Ruth Dennis. Watching Stebbins move, she sees for the first time the individual possibilities of expression and the dignity and truth of the human body. She will call this matinee 'the real birth of my art life,' and take the name Ruth St. Denis.
stops.quote: the real birth of my art life
stops.quote_source: Ruth St. Denis, on seeing Genevieve Stebbins's Dance of Day (1892)
suggested_refs: Ruth St. Denis, Dance of Day and Mystery of Isis
National Christian League for Social Purity matinee program

stops.name: New York — Carnegie Music Hall, the School of Expression founded
stops.campa: In 1893 she founds the New York School of Expression in the Carnegie Music Hall. Norman Astley, once a British Army captain, serves as its business manager. Here the physical-culture women are trained in their hundreds — Felix Adler of the Ethical Society among her pupils; Dr. and Mrs. S. S. Curry of the Boston School of Expression; Dr. C. W. Emerson, founder of Emerson College of Oratory. From this school the harmonic gymnastics spreads through the teachers of a nation. The American station of the notated body has its house.
suggested_refs: New York School of Expression prospectus (1893)

stops.name: New York — Berkeley Lyceum, the picturesque pantomimic matinee
stops.campa: At the Berkeley Lyceum she gives her very picturesque pantomimic matinees; at Madison Square Garden she dances for the Dress Reform Congress, the reformed body made an argument for the reform of women's dress. She lectures and demonstrates without cease, up and down the eastern seaboard with Astley managing the tours. The Greek attitudes, the statue-poses, the breathing drills — she carries them into hall after hall, teaching a generation of American women that the body is an instrument of expression and its freedom a birthright.
suggested_refs: Dress Reform Congress, Madison Square Garden

stops.name: New York — the drama of the greater Eleusinia
stops.campa: Her statue-posing rises to its highest form in what she names the drama of the greater Eleusinia — the ancient mystery of Demeter and Persephone, the descent into darkness and the return of the grain, danced. The living tableaux become a sacred rite; the Greek attitudes are no longer ornament but initiation, the body made a vessel of the old mysteries. Here Delsarte's science of gesture and the yogic breath and the classical form fuse into a mystic dance-drama — the seed of everything the next age will call the dance not yet dreamed.
suggested_refs: Greek attitudes / statue-posing photographs of Stebbins
Eleusinian mysteries of Demeter and Persephone

stops.name: Chautauqua — the platform beside William James
stops.campa: At a Chautauqua conference she stands upon the platform as a speaker beside the philosopher William James, who becomes her friend. The system of the reformed body has become respectable enough to share a rostrum with the founder of American psychology. In these years she publishes The Genevieve Stebbins System of Physical Training, and her drills and Delsartian aesthetic exercises spread through the schools and clubs of the land. She is at the summit of her influence — the most prominent American teacher of the notated, expressive body.
suggested_refs: The Genevieve Stebbins System of Physical Training (1898)

segments.name: Le Mariage Ésotérique — Astley and the Hidden Marriage (1892–1907)

stops.name: Boston — the marriage to Norman Astley
stops.campa: In April 1892, in Boston, she marries Norman Astley — the man who has become her business manager, a former British Army captain. But Astley carries a hidden name. In an earlier life he was Thomas H. Burgoyne, writer of the Hermetic Brotherhood of Luxor, author under the pseudonym Zanoni of its occult correspondence. The marriage joins the priestess of the expressive body to a bearer of the Western esoteric current. Beneath the public work of the school, a second, hidden work begins to turn.

stops.name: Blowing Rock — the retreat in the Blue Ridge
stops.campa: Through these years the Astleys hold land in the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina, in Burke and Watauga Counties — a scenic building lot on the Cliff Rock near Blowing Rock. Between the seaboard tours and the New York school, the high blue mountains are their retreat, the place apart. The public teacher of the body and the hidden hermeticist withdraw here to the hills. The esoteric turn is deepening beneath the surface of the celebrated career; the priestess is preparing to disappear.
suggested_refs: Cliff Rock, Blowing Rock, North Carolina

segments.name: L'Éclipse et le Retour — England and the Vanishing into the Mysteries (1907–1917)

stops.name: New York — the retirement from the School of Expression
stops.campa: In 1907, at the height of her name, she retires from the New York School of Expression and lays down the public work. The matinees, the lecture-demonstrations, the drills — all are set aside. She turns her back on the applause of the Gilded Age and withdraws into the hidden marriage and the hermetic studies. Just as her pupils' pupils are carrying her breath and her attitudes toward Isadora Duncan and Ruth St. Denis and the German Ausdruckstanz, she herself vanishes from the stage of history into the mysteries.
suggested_refs: New York School of Expression, closing (1907)

stops.name: Dittisham, Devon — the crossing to England
stops.campa: The Astleys cross to England and settle first at Dittisham in Devon, on the wooded banks of the Dart. The American priestess of the body becomes an Englishwoman of the hidden path. Here, away from the schools and the halls, she and Astley turn wholly to the inner work — the hermetic studies, the pilgrimage of the spirit. The station of the notated body has closed; what opens now is the station of the invisible one. The great teacher becomes, deliberately, a Pilgrim of the Way.
suggested_refs: Dittisham, Devon, on the River Dart

stops.name: St. Peter Port, Guernsey — the island years
stops.campa: By 1911 the Astleys are on Guernsey, at St. Peter Port in the Channel Islands — a place between two countries, belonging wholly to neither, fit dwelling for a woman who has stepped out of history. Here on the island the hermetic work goes on, half-hidden even from the record. The former celebrity keeps no stage now but the inner one. The rhythm of the tides replaces the rhythm of the matinee; the breath she once taught to hundreds she now breathes for the discipline of her own hidden ascent.
suggested_refs: St. Peter Port, Guernsey, Channel Islands

stops.name: Slindon, Sussex — The Quest of the Spirit
stops.campa: By 1913 the Astleys are settled at Slindon in Sussex, and there is published in London The Quest of the Spirit: by a Pilgrim of the Way — Astley's book, which she edits and owns as her own. 'In editing the work,' she writes, 'I feel that it is the expression of my own thought and aspiration, though voiced by another.' The teacher of the outward body has become the seeker of the inward light; the two lives, public and hidden, are made one in this single volume of the mystic quest.
stops.quote: In editing the work, I feel that it is the expression of my own thought and aspiration, though voiced by another.
stops.quote_source: Genevieve Stebbins, editor's note to The Quest of the Spirit (1913)
suggested_refs: The Quest of the Spirit (Henry Glaisher, London, 1913)

segments.name: El Retorno al Pacífico — California and the Brotherhood of Light (1917–1934)

stops.name: Monterey — the return to the native shore
stops.campa: Before the Great War is out, the Astleys give up their lifelong lease in Sussex and return across the ocean to California — to Monterey, on the Pacific shore of the state where sixty years before she was born. By 1920 they are living on Del Monte Avenue. The great circle is closing: the actress who crossed the whole continent to the New York stage has come home to the far western sea. The public life is long behind her; only the hidden work remains, and the closing of the ring.

stops.name: Carmel-by-the-Sea — the mentors of the Brotherhood of Light
stops.campa: At Carmel-by-the-Sea the Astleys become mentors to the young Elbert Benjamine, and it is they who help draw him to Los Angeles to found the Brotherhood of Light in 1918. Through Astley — through Burgoyne, through Zanoni — the old hermetic current of the Brotherhood of Luxor passes on into the new order, and Stebbins's hidden decades feed its lessons. The teacher of the American body has become, at the last, a mother of an American esoteric church, her influence flowing on unseen as it once flowed into the dance.
suggested_refs: Brotherhood of Light / Church of Light, Los Angeles

stops.name: Monterey — the last certain record
stops.campa: On 21 September 1934, at Monterey, Geneviève Stebbins Astley dies, aged seventy-seven. Her death falls in the very year Elbert Benjamine completes the Brotherhood of Light lessons — the hidden work sealed as her outward life ends. Within a week Astley marries the nurse who tended her, and departs for England. She leaves behind the manuals that are her canon and a lineage she never claimed: the breath and the attitudes she taught, carried by her pupils' pupils, standing at the root of modern dance — the American station between Delsarte and Laban.
